## Choosing Web Hosting in India for a Business, NGO or Online Store: What to Check Before You Pay

The right web hosting for an Indian business website is the one that matches what the site actually does, not the one with the cheapest first-year price. A small brochure site, a WordPress site with a blog, an online store taking orders and an NGO donation site each put different demands on a server, and a plan that suits one can fail the next. Before you buy, check six things: what the plan costs at renewal rather than in year one, whether the server runs a current PHP version, where the server is located, what backups exist and who can restore them, what happens when your traffic outgrows the plan, and whether you control the account and the domain. This guide explains each, and what to ask a host in writing.

We have deliberately changed the shape of this article. An earlier version of this page compared three named hosting companies with speed tests and uptime figures. We could not source those figures to a repeatable test, and hosting plans and prices change several times a year, so we have removed them rather than leave numbers that might mislead you. In their place is a method you can apply to any provider, including ones launched after this was written. Where a price or benchmark would help, we mark a TODO or tell you how to collect it yourself.

### Hosting in one paragraph, for non-technical owners

Your website is a set of files and a database. Web hosting is the rented computer, called a server, that stores them and sends them to anyone who types your address. Your domain name is the address, and it is registered separately from hosting, though many companies sell both. When someone visits, the server finds the files, runs any code needed to build the page and sends the result. How quickly and reliably it does this depends on the server's resources, its software, its location and how many other sites share it.

### The main hosting types, and who each suits

| Type | How it works | Generally suits | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shared hosting | Many sites share one server's resources | Small brochure sites with modest traffic | Limits are often vague; a neighbour's spike can slow you down; may be throttled or suspended under heavy load |
| Managed WordPress hosting | Shared or cloud infrastructure tuned for WordPress, with updates and caching handled | WordPress sites run by a business without a technical team | Plans often cap visits or resources; plugin restrictions; confirm what is included |
| VPS (virtual private server) | A reserved slice of a server with guaranteed resources | Sites with steady traffic, stores, custom applications | Someone must configure, secure, update and monitor it |
| Cloud hosting | Resources drawn from a pool and scaled up or down | Growing stores and applications needing flexibility | Pricing can be hard to predict; needs technical management |
| Dedicated server | A whole physical server for you | Very high-traffic or specialised sites | Cost and management burden; rarely necessary for small businesses |
| Platform-included hosting (Shopify, Wix and similar) | Hosting is part of the subscription | Owners who want no server management | Less control; you work within the platform's rules |

Most small Indian business sites sit in the first two rows. Online stores and donation sites often belong in the managed, VPS or cloud rows, or on a store platform that includes hosting.

### Check one: renewal price, not the first-year price

Hosting is commonly sold with a large discount on the first term, with a much higher price at renewal. Because you will probably stay for more than one term, the figure that matters is the total over the period you expect to use it.

When you compare, build a simple table for each provider: the first-term price, the term length required to get it, the renewal price, the price for a monthly rather than multi-year term, and any extras you need, such as a domain, email or backups. TODO: collect these current figures yourself from each provider's pricing page on the day you decide, since they change. Also check whether the discounted price applies to the full period or only some months.

Be wary of multi-year prepayment for a service you have never used. A one-year term, or a provider that offers a refund window and states its terms plainly, lets you test before committing.

### Check two: software versions

A server is only as safe and fast as the software it runs. For a WordPress site, the project's own [requirements page](https://wordpress.org/about/requirements/) recommends a current PHP version, currently PHP 8.3 or newer, a supported version of MariaDB or MySQL, and HTTPS. It notes older versions still run but have reached end of life and carry security risks.

Ask your host which PHP versions it offers, whether you can choose the version yourself, and what its policy is when a version reaches end of life. A host that offers only old PHP, or cannot tell you, is a risk. Our guide to [PHP end of life and your website](/blog/web-development-company-pune-php-eol-2026/) explains what happens when versions are retired.

Also ask whether HTTPS certificates are included and renew automatically. An expired certificate shows visitors a security warning. Our article on [domain, DNS and SSL renewals](/blog/web-development-company-pune-domain-dns-ssl-renewal-website-downtime-2026/) covers how outages caused by expiry happen and how to prevent them.

### Check three: server location and speed

For visitors in India, a server in or near India generally means a shorter trip for each request than one on another continent. A Content Delivery Network (CDN) can reduce this difference for static files by storing copies near visitors, but the page itself may still come from the origin server.

Do not trust a speed claim in a hosting advertisement or review. Measure for yourself. Put a test site on a trial plan or use a refundable term, then check how quickly the server responds and how the pages perform on a mid-range phone. Google publishes the thresholds it uses for Core Web Vitals; per [web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/defining-core-web-vitals-thresholds), "good" is a Largest Contentful Paint of 2.5 seconds or less, Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less and Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, at the 75th percentile. Hosting affects the first of these most, through server response time. Our guide to [server response time, CDN and caching](/blog/web-development-company-pune-server-response-ttfb-cdn-caching-2026/) shows how to test.

Remember that a poorly built site on excellent hosting is still slow. Heavy images, too many plugins and bulky scripts cost far more time than most server differences, as our guide to [image optimisation](/blog/website-designer-pune-image-optimization-avif-webp-lcp-2026/) explains.

### Check four: backups and who restores them

Almost every host says it has backups. The questions that matter are how often, how long they are kept, where they are stored, whether they are stored somewhere other than the same server, and who restores them and how fast.

- **Frequency.** Daily is a sensible minimum for a site that changes often. A store or donation site that takes orders needs backups that capture recent orders, which may mean more frequent database backups.
- **Retention.** If you discover a problem two weeks after it began, you need a backup older than that.
- **Location.** A backup stored only on the same server disappears if the server fails.
- **Restore process.** Can you restore yourself with a button? Does the host charge to restore? How long does it take?
- **Test.** A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan.

We cover this in depth in our guide to [website backups and disaster recovery](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-backups-disaster-recovery-2026/).

### Check five: what happens at the limit

Every plan has limits, even those advertised as unlimited. Storage, bandwidth, CPU time, memory, number of processes and database connections are typical ones. "Unlimited" usually means a fair-use policy that is written in the terms of service.

Ask in writing: what happens if my site exceeds the plan's limits? Some hosts slow the site, some show an error page and some suspend the account until the next billing period. Also ask about the upgrade path: how quickly can you move to a bigger plan, and does it require migration and downtime?

This matters most for sites that get spiky traffic. A campaign, a festival sale or a media mention can push a small plan past its limits within minutes. If you expect such events, read our article on [whether a donation website can hold up when an appeal goes viral](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-site-traffic-spikes-hosting-load-testing-2026/), which applies equally to any campaign-driven site.

### Check six: ownership and control

The most expensive hosting mistakes are about access, not performance.

- **Who owns the hosting account?** It should be in your business's name, with your email address, and you should hold the login. A developer who buys hosting in their own name and bills you for it holds your website hostage if the relationship ends.
- **Who owns the domain?** Register it yourself, with your own account. See our [handover and ownership checklist](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-handover-ownership-checklist-2026/).
- **Who can log in?** Give your developer their own user, not your password, where the host allows it, and remove access when work ends.
- **Can you take the site elsewhere?** Ask whether you can download full backups of files and database, and whether the host charges to transfer you out.
- **What does the contract say?** Our guide to [contracts, ownership and warranty](/blog/web-development-company-pune-contract-ownership-warranty-2026/) lists the clauses worth reading.

### Support: test it before you need it

Support quality is invisible until something breaks. Before buying, contact the support team with a realistic pre-sales question about migration, PHP versions or limits, and note how quickly and how clearly they answer. Ask what hours support runs, which channels exist, and whether support will help with problems on your site or only with the server.

Also ask what the host does not support. Many managed plans will not debug a plugin or theme, and that is normally the part that breaks.

### Email: keep it in mind

Many hosting plans include business email. Email deliverability depends on correct domain records, and putting marketing email through a shared hosting server can damage your reputation if other users on that server misbehave. Many businesses use a dedicated email service for their staff mailboxes and a separate service for bulk email. Our guide to [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/web-development-company-pune-email-deliverability-spf-dkim-dmarc-2026/) explains the records that keep your messages out of spam folders.

### Hosting for specific kinds of site

#### A simple business or professional website

A clinic, school, consultancy or local firm with a handful of pages usually needs reliable basic hosting, current PHP, a free certificate, backups and good support more than raw power. Managed WordPress hosting or a good shared plan often suffices. Prioritise ownership and backups.

#### An online store

A store has database writes on every order, pages that cannot all be cached, and traffic that spikes around offers. Choose a plan with guaranteed resources, or a store platform that includes hosting. Check backup frequency and the behaviour at the limit. Our guide to [store speed and Core Web Vitals](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-store-speed-core-web-vitals-2026/) lists what to optimise, and our article on [choosing Shopify or WooCommerce](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-shopify-vs-woocommerce-platform-choice-2026/) shows when platform-included hosting makes sense.

#### An NGO donation website

A donation site carries donor data and payments, so reliability, security and backups matter more than a low price. Prefer managed or VPS hosting with documented backups, and plan for campaign spikes. See our guides to [NGO website cost](/blog/ngo-website-cost-india-complete-guide/) and [donor data protection under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026/).

#### A site with large media or heavy traffic

Video, large downloads or heavy traffic call for a CDN and possibly separate media hosting. Do not serve large videos directly from a small shared plan. Use a video platform or a CDN-backed service.

### Common hosting mistakes

**Choosing on first-year price alone.** The renewal price is the real price.

**Buying more than you need.** Many small sites run well on modest plans. Upgrade when measurements show a need.

**Buying less than you need.** A store on the cheapest shared plan can fail in the first sale.

**Never checking backups.** Discover whether they work before you need them.

**Letting the developer hold the account.** Keep it in your name.

**Ignoring software versions.** An outdated PHP version is a security and compatibility risk.

**Forgetting renewal dates.** Add domain, hosting and certificate expiry dates to a shared calendar with more than one person's name on it.

### A pre-purchase checklist

Copy this and ask each provider.

1. What is the price in the first term, at renewal, and on a monthly term?
2. Which PHP versions can I choose, and what is your end-of-life policy?
3. Is HTTPS included and automatic?
4. Where are the servers, and is a CDN available?
5. How often are backups taken, how long kept, where stored, and how do I restore?
6. What are the resource limits, and what happens when I exceed them?
7. How do I upgrade, and is there downtime?
8. Who owns the account, and can I export everything at any time?
9. What support do you provide, through which channels and at what hours?
10. What is not covered by support?

### Worked example: two shops, two answers

Consider two hypothetical Pune businesses. Both are illustrations, not clients.

The first is a physiotherapy clinic with a six-page WordPress site and a contact form. Traffic is modest and predictable. It needs reliable hosting, current PHP, automatic certificates, daily backups with easy restore, and an account in the clinic's own name. A mid-range managed WordPress plan or a good shared plan fits. The owner's priority is not speed tests but making sure the clinic, not the developer, holds the login.

The second is a home decor seller with a WooCommerce store, around a few hundred products and a festival sale each year. Orders write to the database constantly and the sale will spike traffic. A basic shared plan is a risk. A plan with guaranteed resources, a CDN, frequent backups and a written statement of what happens at the limit is a better match, and the owner should run a test of the checkout before the sale. The cost is higher but the downtime risk is lower.

Same technology, different needs. That is the point of matching the plan to the site.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Which web hosting is best for a small business website in India?

There is no single best host. For a small brochure or WordPress site, a reliable managed WordPress or good shared plan with current PHP, automatic HTTPS, daily backups and responsive support usually suffices. Compare the renewal price and make sure the account is in your own name.

### Is cheap shared hosting good enough for a business website?

For a small, low-traffic site it can be, if the host is reliable, keeps software current and backs up daily. It becomes a risk for stores, donation sites and anything with traffic spikes, because resources are shared and limits can slow or suspend the site.

### Do I need an India server for my website?

A server in or near India generally shortens response time for Indian visitors, but it is not the only factor. A CDN, lean pages and good caching matter too. Measure your own site rather than relying on claims.

### Why does my hosting renewal cost so much more than the first year?

Hosts commonly discount the first term heavily to win customers and price renewals higher. Always compare the renewal price and the total over the period you expect to stay, and check whether a monthly or one-year term costs less overall.

### Should my developer buy the hosting for me?

It is fine for the developer to set it up, but the account should be in your business's name with your email and your login. If the developer holds the account, you can lose access to your own website when the relationship ends.

## Where to Start

List what your site does: pages only, or orders and donations too, and whether it faces traffic spikes. Then ask each shortlisted host the ten questions above in writing, and collect the current prices yourself on the day you decide.
